title: Nankana Sahib, 1921
hookLine: reformers seeking to free gurdwaras from corrupt keepers are killed at Guru Nanak's birthplace

lines: A CARETAKER WHO ACTS LIKE THE OWNER.
cards: A family keeps one precious place: the house where a great-great-grandmother was born. The caretaker hired to look after it starts treating it as his own. He charges people to come in and does as he likes inside.

When the family complains, the authorities side with him. What would you do? In the early 1920s, many Sikhs faced that question about their historic gurdwaras, including the one where Guru Nanak was born.

teach.h: AKALI — ONE WHO BELONGS TO THE TIMELESS.
teach.b: Akali means one who belongs to Akal, the Timeless: the old name for God you met at the Akal Takht. In the 1920s it became the name of a movement.
By then many historic gurdwaras were run by mahants, hereditary custodians who had come to treat the shrines and their lands as private property. Some ran them well.
Others let in practices that went against the Gurus' teaching, and some were accused of corruption and worse. The colonial government mostly backed them.

teach.h: JATHAS VOW NOT TO STRIKE BACK.
teach.b: So Sikhs formed jathas, bands of volunteers, to take the gurdwaras back into community care, and they made a vow: no violence, even if attacked.

At dawn on the twentieth of February, 1921, a jatha led by Bhai Lachhman Singh went to Gurdwara Janam Asthan at Nankana Sahib, the place of Guru Nanak's birth, to pray and ask for its handover. The mahant had prepared.

His hired men shut the gates and attacked the Sikhs with guns, swords and axes. The jatha did not fight back. The counts differ: official figures were lower, and Sikh accounts say well over a hundred were killed.

Bhai Lachhman Singh was tied to a tree and burned; the tree still stands at the gurdwara. The news shook all of India. Leaders came from across the country, and the government was forced to act against the mahant.
Within days, the shrine passed into the care of a Sikh committee.
The vow had held: peaceful, and firm.

how: Sikhs remember the martyrs of Nankana Sahib each February, and the jand tree where Bhai Lachhman Singh was killed is preserved at Gurdwara Janam Asthan; pilgrims from India travel there for Guru Nanak's birth anniversary.

games.q: you're in the jatha at Nankana Sahib. the gates shut and armed men attack. you've vowed not to strike back. what happens?
o: the jatha breaks its vow and fights.
the jatha keeps its vow, and many are killed.
the jatha runs, and the vow is forgotten.
games.why: the jatha did not fight back. many were killed, and the news shook all of India.

practice: Recall the last time someone provoked you: a sharp comment, a rude driver, an unfair email.

Picture that moment again, but this time your feet stay planted and your voice stays calm; you don't give up what's right, and you don't strike back. Breathe into that feeling of being steady and unbending at once.
